records.title: Show HN: Petal, open-source CoScreen/ScreenHero finally free
records.author: thedracle
records.storyText:
Hi HN!

I’m Jason Thomas, one of the founders of CoScreen.

As some of you may know, Datadog sunset the CoScreen service on July 31st.

Four of us from the original CoScreen team have spent the last couple months building a free and open source pair programming tool inspired by those that came before us: It’s called Petal (https://github.com/kiruna-labs/petal)

Some history first, because when we started CoScreen we had hoped to break the sad and established pattern of this industry.

Screenhero was an exceptional tool that a lot of us loved for pairing. Multiple cursors, low latency, you could click your partner’s editor, and just start typing. It felt like magic while we had it. Then Slack bought it in 2015, and shut down the standalone app in December 2017.

When Till, Max, and I started CoScreen, we were aware of this history, and wanted to build an even more magical collaboration and screen sharing experience: the entire concept was “throw a window from your laptop up on someone else’s screen, and start collaborating with zero friction.”

Datadog acquired us in 2022, and thus began the great adventure of adapting our real-time technology into Datadog products, while also continue developing CoScreen as a standalone tool from the Datadog ecosystem. Datadog invested in the product for years and we’re thankful for that. But CoScreen itself proved, like so many other screen sharing tool acquisitions, to be too tangential from the customer base and core mission. We instead built other communication features in Datadog, the integrations with other video platforms, and also its wildly successful MCP server. We weren't the only ones. Around was bought by Miro and shut down in March 2025. Multi (formerly Remotion) was acqui-hired by OpenAI in 2024 and shut down about a month later. It's nearly always the same story: a small team builds something hard that people love, a platform buys it for the team or the feature, and the standalone product doesn't survive the integration. So we decided firmly to do things differently this time. Petal is completely free and open source and we aren't monetizing it. If we lose interest or get hit by a bus, you can self-host it or fork it, and nobody can sunset it on you. Honestly it's a love letter to everyone in this community that supported us, believed in us, and to liberate collaborative screen sharing from this vicious cycle.

We hope through this we can help foster a large and vibrant community around innovating in this product sector. What Petal does: shared windows show up as real windows on your desktop, movable and resizable, not tiles in a grid. Several people can share at once, everyone gets a labeled cursor, and you can click into any shared window to type and scroll. Rooms are persistent, so you click once to join "eng-sync" instead of passing links around. It runs on macOS and Windows (Linux is next, this time for real and you can help us!), plus a web app. Media goes over LiveKit. You can use our hosted instance with zero config, or point the app at your own LiveKit server with one docker-compose if you want the traffic to stay on your network or even use an entirely different video backend if you want to. The part that still feels strange to us: CoScreen took almost six years to build. The first version of Petal took under eight weeks, from scratch, with frontier models like Fable and Astra doing a lot of the work. Real-time video and window capture is some of the most unforgiving code we have ever written, so we didn't expect that. We will do a proper writeup on what worked and what didn't, and are happy to answer questions about it here. Till, Darren, Max and I will be in the thread.

records.title: Show HN: I wrote an email app that accepts only one sender per inbox
records.author: edpin2000
records.storyText:
Infinite inboxes, including prefixes where you don't have to create inboxes before you use them -- they self create when you add a suffix.

Three types of inboxes: - One sender. Locks to the first domain to send email (except gmail, outlook, etc where it locks to an email account for obivous reasons. It bounces everyone else. - Temporary. Lasts for a while (24h, 7days, etc) then bounces. Received messages stay or go as per your choice. - Prefix. The most powerful. Declare a prefix like "service" and then invent any suffix, like "service-netflix" or "service$bank" and it creates a new one-sender inbox locked to whoever wrote first.

Bring you own domain. Bring your own AI (MCP server ready). Forwarding.

Please help me test it.

records.title: Show HN: Ito – Build Terminal UIs in Lua
records.author: cat-whisperer
records.storyText:
My friend and I are huge Neovim nerds. We like to rice our terminals and our editors. We just wanted a harness that we can do the same with, rice it till our hearts' desire. So, we started looking out for harnesses. Pi was great, Pi was good. But in the end, it was JavaScript. I don't have anything against JavaScript, but Lua is more fitting, and I can just as easily base it in Rust to make it even faster. So, we started cooking, and we ended up with a design that's minimal at its core and is built using Lua. Every built-in abstraction, the way you define providers, the way you rice it up, everything, literally everything, you can do in Lua.

But how? How does it all work? I proposed we just do it the Ratatui way, but my friend was like, nah! We shall make it possible to build TUIs in Lua. (Weirdo!) But it paid off, and we got ourselves a shiny new Lua library, ito!!!

He didn't get the gravity of the situation. We had an awesome terminal UI library in Lua! I wanted everyone to know how cool that is, so I got cooking, wrote myself a custom canvas implementation of this library instead of the usual terminal adaptor, exported it as wasm, and made this super cool website where you can experiment building awesome UIs in Lua. For vibe-coders, we got an llms.txt too. Have at it, and see if you can build something really cool with it. The library's at github.com/uji-labs/ito, and the awesome sauce harness is at github.com/uji-labs/uji.

I hope you like it!

records.author: bado
records.storyText:
Well, after 15 years of saying "Someday I'll turn this into a web app," I finally did it!

I've been maintaining a popular repo of terminal themes at https://github.com/mbadolato/iTerm2-Color-Schemes, and it was finally time to build the app with all the features I wanted!

I would love for you guys to check it out and provide feedback, feature suggestions, whatever!

And a huge thanks to the community of people that have contributed themes, ports to other terminals, and tools to provide conversions between formats over the years.

Oh! And if you've ever contributed themes to the GitHub repo, please register for an account, find your theme(s), and hit the Claim Authorship button!

records.title: Show HN: BookPress, a WordPress core in C/C++ (Live Demo)
records.author: squareys
records.storyText:
Since ~40% of all websites supposedly still run on WordPress (WP), I thought it might be useful to run it faster. BookPress is about 50% faster than a performance-tuned WP setup with Elementor and WooCommerce.

Every time I used WordPress in the past, I got frustrated how slow it was, even with just a few plugins. So I wrote an light-weight C/C++ core and an embeddable PHP engine to run plugins and themes, with most of the WP API surface covered.

Try the live demo, including wp-admin!

The embeddable PHP runtime that covers most of Zend PHP's features runs 2x slower than Zend, but BookPress is still faster than a performance-tuned WP instance with OPCache, page cache and object caches.

BookPress runs alongside a traditional WP installation on Linux arm64 and x86_64.

Looking forward to what you all think.

Every day, I let all frontier AI models play five rounds of an image location guess game. Try it out how you perform against the AI.

I recently released my browser image location game, a hobby project where you’re get random images from sources like Wikimedia Commons and have to guess the image’s location. My goal was to make this online catalog playable and to make it easier to discover new places and Wikipedia articles. I realize I’m certainly not the first person to have this idea, but I’ve tried to build a cohesive overall concept around it with multiplayer, content filter, own image collections and more.

I thought it would be interesting to see how well AI models do at guessing images, and I have to say, they're very good. To make it a little more interesting, every user can also take a guess at each image. I hope you find it interesting and enjoy guessing. I know it's not really a fair comparison. records.author: daniel_tenuo

Tenuo is a task-scoped authz primitive for agentic work. We are an open protocol and an open source implementation at github.com/tenuo-ai/tenuo

We created a fork of OWASP finbot with Tenuo wired in and red-teamed it with promptfoo. We went from 50 successful attacks to 0 with Tenuo.

The promptfoo attacks were able to fool the model, but the deterministic guardrails Tenuo provides stopped it from acting on the poisoned instructions.

records.title: Show HN: GitVolt, open source fast Git GUI (Tauri/CEF)
records.author: francislavoie
records.storyText:
Hi HN!

I've been working on this for the past few weeks. I've been using GitKraken for a whole 10 years now, and I've always loved it, but lately I've found it to be a bottleneck, and I haven't seen it improve the features I really care about. So, as many others have done recently, I took a shot at using Opus 5.5 to help me build my dream Git GUI app.

I did take massive inspiration from GitKraken (the look and feel is a close match since it's what I feel comfortable with) but everything is built from scratch. I made lots of different UX choices that I think help streamline things.

Most importantly, performance was the key thing to get right at the start. I daily-drive Linux so that was first. I went with Tauri to have a really fast Rust core, and after doing performance testing with WebKitGTK it wasn't good enough. So I'm using Tauri's v3 alpha with CEF (Chromium) which made it easy to get a butter smooth 60fps for scrolling a huge list of commits (whereas I would barely get 10fps in my large repo with GitKraken, with tons of hitching). Everything feels so much faster.

The website is best viewed on desktop, I included a fully functional web-only version of the app (mocked git and gitlab) so you can try it out!

Some cost numbers: ~16 billion tokens, ~$5.4k at API rates, 5.2 full weekly quotas (spread over two 5x plans), ~$120 of subsidized plan cost.

records.title: Show HN: TowerPanic – a family party game on a small FastAPI realtime engine
records.author: ms209495
records.storyText:
I want to show you the game I created recently and tell you whole the story/experience - including backend/latency/scalability.

You can try it quickly without an account - I created game demo rooms (EU/US/JP) - links below - just be aware that anyone with a link can access join the game.

Let's start with short description of the game itself:

This is the TowerPanic game - you are standing on one of four towers, during each round some of towers crack, and some of these lean, and finally one of these colapse - you need to watch out to not be on the failing one. It's a multiplayer game for whole family. This can be also used as an icebreaking game - for people in any age. The game is safe for children - no violence, no strangers, no chat, no ads. Parent creates an account (free 14-day trial, then a paid pass) and starts the game - others join using a QR code or a link.

Behind the game there is an interesting backend engine - I willdescribe it in a moment.

Let's start with the history of this whole project: - I was playing with asyncio and fastapi - As an exercise I created a reliable chat application (multiple rooms, in each room each user can reliably broadcast a message to all other users) - I extracted communication to separate layer - creating network/application layer interfaces - 'reliable client' interface for client and 'state machine' interface for the service on server. - With these interfaces - I was able to create other service - an 'sgame' (simple game). With verified interfaces and created services (chat, sgame) I was able to ask AI to generate other tools/games - I was impressed by these results - the games/tools worked well - I deployed them on a remote server - I was surprised that the latency was very good - almost everything worked smoothly

I tested the tools and games with my children and one of the game was really great. I decided to make this game public - I chose 'TowerPanic' name for it.

I prepared an account/payment server for this game (as a separate FastAPI application). This was very good choice: - the game servers keep rooms only in memory - nothing persistent (rooms have expiration date) - the account server keeps all persistent data (it uses database)

Because of this split I was able to figure out how to upgrade and scale frontend and backend independently - without significantly impacting users.

I optimized the communication layer - so that it works in finite memory - only finite number of recent messages is kept, and I sent a full service snapshot (full state) to the lagging clients.

The backend process (FastAPI/python) is limited by python GIL (only one core can be utilized) - to utilize all server cores I used HAProxy with consistent hashing to distribute rooms - so that users can be redirected to proper backend process.

I tested how many rooms a single server can handle - it handles hundreds of active rooms in parallel with no significant latency drop.

Before making it public I noticed that latency in other region of world might be higher and this could influence UX - I confirmed this using artificial delay on my remote server.

I decided to deploy the application in three regions - EU, US, JP - to ensure low latency (below 150ms) in most of the world. The room is created in region closest to the user (best latency from the browser to backend).

I needed also to prepare some legal documents (terms, privacy, refunds) - thanks to AI this was much easier. I'm a backend engineer, frontend/UI/UX were designed by me but code was generated by AI.

To summerize all this work: - I'm happy that I was able to deliver complete game/complete product - I think the whole work took me about 20 evenings - I'm impressed that it was so short - I think this is because the technology I used is popular and all fits well - AI was great as a peer (to discuss the options for distributing the load, discuss were to locate servers, or discuss how auth/payments work under the hood, ... - based on this I could choose the best option) - AI was great for doing the non work which I'm doing ineffectively (frontend/UI/legal docs).

The game is available at https://towerpanic.com/?ref=hn

I will appreciate your comments/feedback:

Product: - did you meet any obstacles to play ? - how smoothly it worked ? - please specify your location if it didn't work well - most important thing/things to improve ? - anything else ... Solution/Engineering: - one thing you will change in the architecture / approach ? - anything else ...

records.title: Show HN: Fantastic Canvas
records.author: Alexadar
records.storyText:
Fantastic is my own harness. It runs on an Erlang-like, OS-like meta-runtime instead of agent loops or agent graphs.

I believe this is the right design for an AI runtime: it puts humans, AI agents and tools on equal footing.

It will grow into a convenient multi-OS runtime that can do what other AI libraries and harnesses do. For now it’s a technical demo with two modes: a CLI coder, and a spatial canvas that’s very handy for a lot of everyday work.

I think the canvas mode is the kind of software we’ll all be using in the 2030s.

I don’t have a name for it yet, so for now let’s call it “emergent software”. The idea is that you build, run and engineer your own systems visually, with help from AI, inside your own dynamic interface that you build for yourself. It’s a lot of fun, especially for multimedia projects.

For example, in a canvas project I’m still working on, a third-party AI agent generates UI and agents: it builds a control panel for making a Manim animation, and a viewport for a Blender video built from the Manim animation’s guidelines. I’ll record a video later; for now I just want to share the general idea. Maybe someone will like it.

If anyone wants to talk about it more, let me know in the comments and I’ll respond.

Have a fantastic day!

Oleksandr

records.title: Show HN: Run AI-generated logic safely inside your app
records.author: cj-builds
records.storyText:
Stof is an open-source runtime for logic you don't own or fully trust.

Imagine a JSON document with functions inside, scoped to just the document that contains them. Stof instantiates this doc as a small wasm env, and makes these functions safe to call. They can't access or manipulate anything but their own doc.

WebAssembly by itself is large in binary form, requires a lot of tooling, etc. Stof can be sent over the wire easily, is a superset of JSON for compatibility, and keeps the guarantees.

I created Stof not to replace a data format or anything, but to be a glue layer for data and distributed systems to work with one another. This includes I/O for interchange data like JSON, YAML, TOML, etc., but also complex data like PDFs, images, binaries, both structured and unstructured (good layer to turn one into the other).

The fact is, the layer of data and communication between apps tends to be a bit messy, and strict adapters compiled at build time tend to be insufficient for the dynamism of modern software.

This applies directly to AI-generated data and code, which is basically like calling into another untrusted service. With this, you can safely embed the execution, pick where things run, and combine harnesses like data. Works well as a "living" context, also with the JSON interop - just parse into or stringify sections of the Stof doc at runtime when needed, like agent tool defs.

The playground on the site runs entirely in your browser. Stof is written in Rust and has support for JS/TS and Python today.

I'd especially like feedback on whether the idea makes sense from the landing page, and where the docs need help.

GitHub: https://github.com/dev-formata-io/stof

Thank you!!

-CJ

records.title: Show HN: Eevo – Consequential Decision Model
records.author: ojalajuho
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Juho from Upright. I think we may have stumbled upon an interesting approach to AI alignment.

The idea is as follows: 1. train a decision model to be really good at comparative sizing of consequences, expected value problems, and modelling overlap between different consequences 2. create a harness around that model that accepts a decision context, list of options, and identified consequences, then runs pairwise comparisons and overlap modelling for the consequences using the decision model in (1), and finally solves implied relative consequences "sizes" and finally EV (for different stakeholders) 3. Make AI agents running on general purpose LLMs use (2) to make better decisions. So the agent provides the context, options, and identifies the consequences, Eevo model just sizes them, models their overlap, and computes EV.

In practice this seems to improve agent judgement a lot (in addition to adding lots of practical observability)

It seems the (well-motivated) emphasis on instruction-following hurts model's performance on expected value tasks. The underlying decision model we trained beats Jev, Clef, MS decision-1 the model on OpenAI decisions API on economic rationality benchmarks like STEEP, expected value tasks, poker, and even Pacman (Jevman benchmark). I swear to you we did not Benchmaxx on Pacman

Also it seems to be useful also for human decisions. Just getting other people's decisions presented to you in standard format with consequences listed and sized is just very pleasant. There are some testers though who think this is useful for improving everyone's judgement, except their own

Hello HN, I am Kartikeya & we are building the best AI Slop Detector - Checkobot.

Current AI Image Detectors are functionally jagged. Some are not able to detect deepfakes, some fail on the latest flux models. Some have an unacceptable false flag rate on genuine images.

We have been solving the deepfake detection problem at our parent company - SpoofSense.ai for a while now & we wanted to train a general purpose AI Image Detector that actually works.

Checkobot does 3 things: 1.Full Image Model - Detect for AI generator signals in the entire image. 2. Face Specialist - Focuses only on the face to spot face-swaps, edits. 3. C2PA - Checks if the file has signed Content Credentials that record AI generation or editing.

Free checks are processed in memory and not stored; we keep the SHA-256 and the verdict. 3 free checks a day.

I'd like to hear where it gets things wrong, especially images it misses or flags unfairly.

records.storyText:
Over the last 20 years, I repeatedly got frustrated with how slow WordPress (WP) is, especially once you stack a few plugins on it.

Since 40% or what of all websites still run on WP, I decided [and please don't ask why, I have no idea what drove me] it could be useful to apply my C/C++ performance experience to a brand new from-scratch WP core to save about 50% of infrastructure while simultaneously increasing performance. With agent assisted coding I thought it could actually be doable to build out most of WP' API surface, and it was! (over multiple months)

Try the live demo, including wp-admin!

It shows WooCommerce + Elementor working, which is remarkable because I had to build an embeddable PHP runtime that covers most of Zend PHP's features for it. Runs 2x slower than Zend, but BookPress is still faster than a performance-tuned WP instance with OPCache, page cache and object caches.

I don't mean to replace WP, and am faithfully implementing the API to avoid any divergence or "BookPress" handling in plugins or themes. BookPress is meant to run alongside a PHP WP installation, with a single-command migrate and un-migrate.

Looking forward to what you all think.

records.title: Show HN: Earshot – old smartphone can listen to smoke alarm, doorbell or dog
records.author: hessdalenlight
records.storyText:
TLDR: I’m building Earshot - the sound detection app that can detect (ideally) any sound described by text.

The neural model under the hood is a CLAP-style model (CLIP for audio): basically during the training you force the model make inner text and audio representations to match. And then you can use such model as 0-shot audio classifier. For POC I used LAION’s clap-htsat model but it turned out to be quite "heavy" so I’ve trained a smaller one by myself.

As for text encoder I used model from the EfficientAT family; for audio I used jhu-clsp/ettin-encoder-32m. The training was performed on my mighty 2x1080 Ti home server. The trained weights can be found on my HF: https://huggingface.co/mirth/earshot-clap-mn10-ettin32

I would appreciate it if you could test this application (especially if you could report if an app missed the sound).

A couple of disclaimers:

1. The sound never leaves you device.

2. It can miss the sound so it’s not a replacement for your monitoring system (but an extra pair of ears).

3. I’m aware that similar functionality is presented in the Apple HomePod but there is a minor difference: to add very custom sound for detection on HomePod you need first to record it (to train inner HomePod model I presume). In my case you can just describe the sound in the text format.

Happy to answer any questions!

records.title: Show HN: Are interstellar visitors alien probes?
records.author: Lucent
records.storyText:
There was a lot of debate about whether the 3 interstellar objects found might not be natural. Most of it cherry-picked a few oddities and claimed decisively, for or against. I don't have a strong opinion, and don't trust my eye for coincidence or to spot astrology-like "planetary alignment", so I simulated millions of random paths through the solar system and counted how many came closer than the 3 known objects, either to the planets or to or from nearby stars.

1I and 2I look like chance. Loeb et al. put 3I's planetary passes at 1 in 20,000. Scored against all eight planets and random arrivals of its speed, it's about 1 in 300. I don't know how much more easily surveys spot objects along the ecliptic, which would explain some of 3I's coincidence.

I welcome forking the project and adjusting the assumptions I made, like a Bracewell or von Neumann probe would take a traveling salesman path, or that it would need to fly near multiple planets.

It's a hobby project I do on my free time, so there are rough edges (particularly around search), however I’d appreciate any feedback or suggestions!

records.title: Show HN: Nexus – open-source local-first message routing for agents
records.author: earldennison
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I built Nexus because I was tired of having multiple agents that I had to address one by one. I built an underlying mechanism where I could message all of them and have them have the capability to message each other and listen to wake events. I also got tired of having to run cron when I think that agents should have the capability to be event-driven.

Nexus is basically a daemon that runs and routes messages to where they need to be, it is fully customizable, which you can write scripts off of so that it will wake agents or route that message to an already existing agent. Right now it supports Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode and Hermes. But more are underway. It runs on your machine with no container required. (In my opinion, messaging within your machine should not require you to have to run a container.)

To try it:

  npm install --global @egregore/nexus
It runs on Linux, Windows and WSL today; It can run on mac but I havent fully tested it also you would have to build the binaries yourself for the latest version though. Full support for it is planned in the near future.

records.title: Show HN: Face, a browser window over agents that keeps the plan in files
records.author: JCKodel
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm the author. FACE is a single Go binary. You run `face` in the folder that holds your projects and it serves a page on 127.0.0.1. It speaks ACP (the Agent Client Protocol that Zed published) to the official CLI of the agent you already use: Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Cursor, OpenCode, Qwen Code or Antigravity, signed in with your own account. FACE has no model, no key and no agent loop of its own.

Why I built it: a coding agent ships a feature in an afternoon, and three people and five sessions later nobody can answer "what is in flight, what did it cost, why was it decided this way". The answer I landed on is not a dashboard but a method where every decision and every delivery is a versioned file: a handful of docs written once, a queue with one line per delivery (docs/06), and one page per delivery (work/<slug>.md) that says what will be built and how it is proven before any code changes. The method is four slash commands the agent reads from one file (brainstorm, analyze, propose, apply); it works without FACE. FACE is the window: the queue becomes a five-lane board, a card opens into the page plus the live session, and the commit window shows exactly what the agent staged. The agent never commits or merges; you click.

I built FACE itself with it, from the fourth week on. Before that the same method shipped a job marketplace in 89 one-page deliveries over 14 days, and a consulting project in 107 deliveries over 19 days.

Install: `brew install jckodel/face/face`, `winget install JCKodel.FACE`, a `.deb`, or `curl -fsSL https://face.kodel.com.br/install.sh | sh`. macOS, Linux, Windows, arm64 and amd64. UI in en, pt, es, fr, de and zh-Hans.

What is missing: single user and local only (a team mode with a server on your network is the next milestone); no editor (it shows code and diffs, your editor stays your editor); the source is not public yet. It will be visible under a fair source license when the paid tier for teams exists, and the free tier stays free. By itself FACE makes at most two requests, both off until you turn them on: a daily anonymous ping that counts machines and a daily version check. The page "What FACE sends" lists both URLs.

Happy to answer anything about ACP, the adapters for Claude and Codex (they are not ACP native, so FACE wraps them), or the method.

records.title: Show HN: Working on Plug and play AI memory that works across AI agents
records.author: heysrb
records.storyText:
So I've been working on a project (Make0 AI) for a long time where I wanted to give common context to both Codex and Claude Code. The problem is simple - while working on Claude and after exhausting the daily/weekly limits I've start again from scratch in Codex. Of course I can prompt Claude to summarise a handoff that I can give to Codex but that is inefficient. So I thought of a creating a common context for both of them locally using a simple list of instructions like a shared md file. But the problem was the file kept on growing and after some point the common context went beyond 20k tokens and was just inflating the token budget unnecessarily.

Then I implemented a RAG based retrieval approach on the list to only load what is required for that prompt and voila, after a few more iterations it resulted into a graph memory - Brain.

So this product Make0 AI gives you the ability to create Brains that you can connect to any Ai agent via MCP and then they immediately know your likes, dislikes, preferences etc. AI agents can read, write to this memory.

This can be your long term memory and the agents just become the token providers and task executors. You have full control over your data/memories from a single place. Think of this as a "USB thumb drive brain" that you plug to any agent.

I know I may not be the first one to implement this but I tried to make the UX simple and is not at all developer focused. You can just drag and drop your memories/data to the brain and even play around with a visual brain.

One more thing, i've done benchmarks on the memory. LoCoMo scores 83.3% overall, with Single hop 92.5% in standard mode (available now) and in another configuration (experimental max mode) it scores 92% overall and 94.4% in single hop. Available in the benchmark page. It uses hybrid search + graph memory and has built in conflict resolution for memories.

Do let me know if you folks wanna try it!

records.title: Show HN: Real Design Benchmark – can you tell AI designs from real products?
records.author: ginzberg
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

I'm Adam Ginzberg, one of the cofounders of Subframe, a code-first design tool.

One of the things I'm really curious about is understanding LLM performance on subjective domains like design.

As an experiment I built this game which presents two designs of the same screen, one of which was generated by AI. First you pick which one you like better and then which one you think was made by AI.

Most design work happens in an existing product, so we set up this game to test that. As context, the AI gets 4 screenshots from the existing product, the product's icons + fonts, and a written brief about the screen it is asked to build. It then writes HTML which is screenshotted identically to the real screen. To get the data, we signed up for the products with test accounts and added dummy data. All of the inputs were manually checked to make sure nothing about the target screen was leaked in the prompt. You can read more about the methodology at https://www.realdesignbenchmark.com/methodology.

After a few thousand submissions, the surprising result is that people prefer the AI design - 57% prefer AI, 33% prefer the real design, 10% say they are about the same. People are also not great at identifying the AI design, only 59% get it right.

The initial results were all generated with Opus 5.5 (medium effort). We just added GPT-6.1 Sol (medium effort) tonight.

Give the game a try. Feedback on the approach is appreciated. Or any ideas on what we might improve or try next.

Hi HN,

I'm a sound editor and composer. I had an MPE (MIDI Polyphonic Expression) keyboard sitting on the desk in front of me and not enough space for a DAW control surface. About a year later, I have an 8-channel control surface running on HUI or Mackie Control with all major functions, including a system wide keyboard shortcut and macro engine.

The crucial part was getting the keys to respond like a real fader, starting in the right position when touched and not introducing jumps or jitters into the mix. The result is really smooth control though, and it works better than I originally imagined it would.

It's macOS only for now, and works with ROLI Seaboard models and KMI K-board Pro. It should also work with Haken Continuum, but is not tested.

DAWs tested and confirmed: Pro Tools, Logic Pro, Cubase, Studio One, Reaper, Ableton Live and Digital Performer, plus video editors using the same protocols, such as DaVinci Resolve's Fairlight page.

records.title: Show HN: Beaniebrand – Easy way to create a cute logo for your product
records.author: jayanthputta
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Jayanth. Beaniebrand helps you generate a cute logo + interactive mascot for your brand/product/company. You describe your product, and it generates 4 different logo + mascot combinations to choose from. You can then describe changes in plain english.

Once you find one you like, you get a downloadable kit with:

- SVG and PNG logos, icons, and favicons in multiple sizes and colors - An animated React mascot with multiple expressions that can react to what's happening in your app (think Clippy!) - An agent skill so your coding agent knows how to add the kit to your app and use it

You can see our own mascot guiding you around the homepage too :)

The problem: As I built and shipped apps of various kinds, I noticed I'd get stuck trying to find a logo that I liked. I'd go back and forth with Claude/Codex or try using tools like Looka. Then came the SVGs, different icon sizes, color variations, favicons, and so on.

Would love feedback! It takes a few minutes to generate the options but the wait is worth it :)

records.title: Show HN: Collaborative money tracker, E2E encryption, MCP
records.author: bandrw
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Andrei. I built a money tracker for myself with everything I ever wanted from one.

What was important for me is wallets in different currencies (I travel a lot), planning future payments, seeing what balances would look like at certain date in the future and having external API and MCP.

I had plans of maybe making it public one day so I decided to encrypt amounts and balances to stand out from gazillion of other trackers, then I kept adding more stuff like semantic search, charts, shared wallets for collaboration, passkey-only sign in and so on.

It's a web app, I use it as PWA and it works fine for now. Native mobile apps are worth making only if there is demand, so current stack is Nextjs, Hono, Postgres, a VPS and Cloudflare.

I'd love feedback, especially on encryption and collaboration part and what would make you switch from your current tracker.
